name: Looking after someone with dementia
headline: Looking after someone with dementia: what the NHS advises
summary: The NHS suggests simple communication, steady routines and home aids, and advises carers to ask the council for a free carer's assessment.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests speaking slowly in short sentences, keeping eye contact and giving the person time to answer.
The NHS says a sudden change in behaviour or sudden confusion may point to a health problem such as an infection.
A carer's assessment from the council is free, and anyone over 18 can ask for one.
A lasting power of attorney lets a person choose someone they trust to act for them, and sources advise making one while the person can still decide.
In an emergency or if anyone is in immediate danger, call 999.

body.heading: How can I talk with someone who has dementia?
body.body:
NHS guidance suggests speaking slowly in short sentences and keeping eye contact. It also suggests giving the person time to answer without rushing them. Offering simple choices, or asking a question in a different way, can help. Cutting down background noise, such as a loud television or radio, and not interrupting are also suggested. When speech becomes harder, body language and gentle touch can matter more.

For repeated questions, the NHS says reassurance can ease things, and a visible answer such as an easy-to-read clock may help. It suggests listening for a theme behind the question, such as the person believing they are lost, and offering reassurance.

body.heading: What helps with daily routines and safety at home?
body.body:
NHS Inform Scotland recommends a regular daily routine, which it says can encourage feelings of security, value and worth. Daily walks are suggested for restlessness, and they can also help with sleep and bowel regularity. Letting the person help with simple jobs, such as laying the table or shopping, can help them feel useful. For sleep, the advice includes plenty of daylight and activity during the day, no caffeine or alcohol in the evening, and limiting daytime naps.

Memory aids can be used around the home, such as pictures on cupboard doors showing what is inside. Other suggestions include keeping keys in one place and writing reminders to lock the door at night or turn the gas off. For wandering, the NHS suggests going with the person on walks or considering telecare, such as tracking devices and alarms. An occupational therapist might be able to suggest changes to the home to help with daily routines.

body.heading: Why might behaviour change, and what can help?
body.body:
The NHS says that if a change in behaviour comes on suddenly, the cause may be a health problem. It advises asking a GP for an assessment to rule out or treat any underlying cause. Alzheimer's Society lists constipation, pain and urinary tract infections as common triggers. It also suggests asking the GP to review all the person's medicines, including any bought without a prescription.

When someone is aggressive, the NHS suggests trying to stay calm and avoiding confrontation. Doctors may check for uncontrolled pain, untreated depression, infections and side effects of medicines. The NHS adds that specialists may prescribe an antipsychotic medicine if coping strategies do not work and the person has persistent aggression or extreme distress.

body.heading: What if confusion comes on suddenly?
body.body:
Sudden confusion is different from the slow changes of dementia, and the NHS says it needs medical help straight away. The NHS advises calling 999 for sudden confusion rather than driving the person to A&E. It lists infection as a common cause, with urinary tract infections frequent in older people and people with dementia. Stroke or a mini-stroke (TIA) and low blood sugar in people with diabetes are other causes it names.

Alzheimer's Society advises that if you think a person with dementia has delirium, you call the GP or NHS 111 straight away. NHS trusts say delirium can look like a sudden change from the person's usual behaviour. They add that delirium can be mistaken for dementia getting worse, and that finding and treating the cause early gives a better outcome.

body.heading: What support is there for the person doing the caring?
body.body:
The NHS says a carer can ask for an assessment to see what might make life easier, and it is free for anyone over 18. It is arranged through the local council's adult social services. The assessor asks how caring affects the carer's physical and mental health, work, free time and relationships. A carer can have one even if the person they care for does not want their own needs assessed.

An assessment might recommend someone to take over caring so the carer can take a break, training in how to lift safely, or help with housework and shopping. The NHS also advises carers to register as a carer with their GP. Admiral Nurses are specialist dementia nurses who give practical and emotional support to carers, and in some areas the NHS provides them with the charity Dementia UK. Alzheimer's Society runs a Dementia Support Line and an online forum where carers can talk to others.

body.heading: How can a family plan ahead?
body.body:
The NHS describes a lasting power of attorney (LPA) as a legal document that lets a person choose someone they trust to act on their behalf. There are two kinds, one for property and financial affairs and one for health and welfare. A person can make one or both, and can choose the same attorneys or different ones. GOV.UK says LPAs are not only a way to plan for losing mental capacity through dementia.

The forms must be signed to confirm the person has mental capacity and be witnessed, and each LPA is then registered with the Office of the Public Guardian. Several sources stress acting early, while the person can still make these decisions. Without an LPA, family members may have to apply to the Court of Protection to become a deputy, which can take time and be costly. The NHS page says a solicitor is not required, and suggests the Law Society directory and the Office of the Public Guardian for help.

body.heading: Where can I get urgent help if things become too much?
body.body: Caring can be hard on the carer, and help is available at any time. If someone is in immediate danger or at risk of serious self-harm, call 999. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which NHS pages describe as open 24 hours a day. Anyone can call on behalf of someone else, and the call is free. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
